title: Royal Bank of Scotland Headquarters
about_landmark_text: Designed by Sir William Chambers and completed in 1774 as a private townhouse for Sir Lawrence Dundas, this Palladian mansion became the Scottish Excise Office in 1795 before the Royal Bank of Scotland acquired it in 1825. It remains the bank's registered head office today.
about_subject_text: The domed banking hall was added in 1857 by architect John Dick Peddie, its ceiling ringed with star-shaped skylights trimmed in gold. Sir Lawrence Dundas, who commissioned the original house, was one of the wealthiest men in Georgian Scotland - his fortune was built substantially on the transatlantic slave trade.
interesting_fact: The domed ceiling of the banking hall is famous enough to have been featured on Royal Bank of Scotland banknotes.

puzzle_explanation: The "green man" is William Pitt the Younger, whose weathered bronze statue has stood on Hanover Street since shortly after his death in 1806.
about_landmark_text: Sculpted by Sir Francis Chantrey, this statue has stood at the corner of George Street and Frederick Street since 1833 - one of several statesmen honoured along Edinburgh's New Town streets.
about_subject_text: Pitt became Prime Minister in 1783 aged just 24 - still the youngest in British history. A contemporary joke dubbed his government a "mince-pie administration" that wouldn't survive Christmas. It lasted 17 years. He went on to lead Britain through most of the wars against Napoleonic France and introduced the country's first income tax in 1798, before dying in office in 1806, aged just 46.
interesting_fact: In 1798 he fought a pistol duel with fellow MP George Tierney on Putney Heath - both men deliberately missed their shots, and honour was declared satisfied.

puzzle_explanation: Bute House, 6 Charlotte Square, has been the official residence of Scotland's First Minister since 1999.
about_landmark_text: Designed by Robert Adam as part of his grand vision for Charlotte Square in 1791 - though Adam died the following year, before it was finished. Number 6 has been the official residence of Scotland's First Minister since 1999.
about_subject_text: The plot was first sold in 1792 to Orlando Hart, a shoemaker and prominent Edinburgh town councillor. The building later spent nearly 20 years as a hotel, and the Marquesses of Bute owned it for over 60 years before it was preserved for the nation in 1966.
interesting_fact: In 1832, the exiled King Charles X of France stayed here briefly while it was operating as a hotel - some of the hotel's original brass lettering is still visible on the building today.

title: Wojtek the Soldier Bear Memorial
address: West Princes Street Gardens, Edinburgh (near Castle Street terrace path)
clue_text: head 440m as the crow flies on heading 128(Southeast). Alas you are not a crow and will need to walk, but there are multiple routes to get there. You are looking for an animal you already saw today - don�t forget to note what you see on the way, you will need it for the quiz
about_landmark_text: Unveiled on 7 November 2015, the memorial is the work of Scottish sculptor Alan Beattie Herriot and was cast at Powderhall Bronze in Edinburgh. A bronze soldier of the 2nd Polish Corps walks beside Wojtek at one-and-a-quarter life size, one hand resting on the bear's back. Behind them a low curved granite wall carries a four-metre bronze relief panel tracing Wojtek's wartime journey. It sits on the terrace path in West Princes Street Gardens, below the castle rock near Castle Street.
about_subject_text: Wojtek was a Syrian brown bear cub, bought from a boy in Iran in 1942 by Polish soldiers on their way to the war. He grew up inside the 22nd Artillery Supply Company, drinking beer, wrestling the men and eating cigarettes. Barred from British troopships as a pet, he was formally enlisted with a paybook and the service number 253. At Monte Cassino in 1944 he is said to have carried crates of artillery shells. He was demobbed in Scotland and died at Edinburgh Zoo in 1963.
interesting_fact: The granite the pair stand on was quarried at Strzegom in Poland and shipped to Edinburgh, so that the soldier and his bear would always have a piece of their homeland underfoot.

title: The Scott Monument
clue_text: look east-north-east for a land mark of note - then head towards it - dont forget to note what you see on the way, you will need it for the quiz
puzzle_question: What is the first name of the bloke at the bottom?
about_landmark_text: A Victorian Gothic spire of pale Binny sandstone, built 1840-44 and standing 61.1 metres tall. Visitors can climb 287 steps through four viewing platforms to look out over the city. Around its base and up its sides sit 68 carved statuettes of characters from Scott's novels, and a white marble statue of Sir Walter Scott himself by John Steell.
about_subject_text: Its architect wasn't a trained architect at all. George Meikle Kemp was a self-taught joiner and draughtsman who entered the 1836 design competition under the pseudonym 'John Morvo' - the name of Melrose Abbey's medieval master mason - expecting his lack of credentials to sink his chances. He won, but never saw it finished: walking home from the site on a foggy night in March 1844, he fell into the Union Canal and drowned.
interesting_fact: The monument's famous black colour isn't the stone's own - Binny sandstone is naturally pale. A century and a half of coal smoke from 'Auld Reekie' is what turned it dark.

title: Fleshmarket Close
address: Market St & Fleshmarket Cl, Edinburgh EH1 1DE

about_landmark_text: Fleshmarket Close is a steep, narrow medieval alley climbing from Market Street, just behind Waverley Station, up to Cockburn Street and the High Street above. It takes its name from the flesh (meat) market once held here: butchers hung carcasses along the passage, with blood running down the slope toward the old Nor Loch that used to fill the valley now occupied by Princes Street Gardens. The market had moved here from beside the Tron Kirk by the late 17th century. Today the close remains one of the most-used routes between the railway station and the Old Town, its stone stair still climbing between the same close-set tenement walls.
about_subject_text: The close lent its title to Fleshmarket Close, the fifteenth Inspector Rebus novel by Edinburgh crime writer Ian Rankin, published in 2004. It was also long home to the Jinglin' Geordie pub - named after the 17th-century Edinburgh goldsmith and moneylender George Heriot - which for decades was a favourite watering hole for journalists from the Evening News and The Scotsman, until both papers moved out to Holyrood in 1999.
interesting_fact: In June 2025 the close was among several Old Town locations used to film J. J. Abrams's The Great Beyond (shot under the working title Ghostwriter), starring Glen Powell, Jenna Ortega, Emma Mackey and Samuel L. Jackson, with release expected in November 2026.

title: Tron Kirk Market
clue_text: take the steps (you may want to count them) - turn at the top and follow the road - you are looking for a market place - dont forget to note what you see on the way, you will need it for the quiz
puzzle_question: How many stained glass windows with arched tops?
about_landmark_text: The Tron Kirk's foundation stone was laid on 4 March 1637, commissioned by King Charles I after St Giles' up the street was made Edinburgh's cathedral and its parish needed a church of its own. It was designed by John Mylne, the crown's master mason, in a style blending Gothic tracery with Dutch-influenced classical detailing, and wasn't fully finished until the 1640s because of the upheavals of the Wars of the Covenant. Its original steeple was destroyed in the Great Fire of Edinburgh in November 1824; the current spire, by architects R. & R. Dickson, replaced it in 1828. The congregation held its final service here on 21 September 1952, after which it merged with St Giles', carrying its seventeenth-century communion silver up the street in procession.
about_subject_text: The kirk takes its name from the tron, a public weighing beam that stood on the High Street outside it until around 1800, used to weigh and tax goods sold nearby - a reminder that this stretch of the Royal Mile has been a marketplace for centuries longer than the church itself has stood here. After decades as a council-run heritage centre and tourist information point, the building reopened on 1 July 2022 as Tron Kirk Market, run by the Scottish Design Exchange, where local Scottish makers sell jewellery, art and craft work from stalls inside the old nave.
interesting_fact: Restoration work in the 1970s uncovered the cobbled surface of Marlin's Wynd beneath the church floor - a paved street thought to be among the oldest in Scotland, named after the mason Walter Merlioun, who lived there around 1500. Part of it has been left visible under glass panels in the floor.

title: Deacon Brodies Tavern
clue_text: head up the royal mile - you are looking for a burglar!  - dont forget to note what you see on the way, you will need it for the quiz
puzzle_question: How old was he when he died?
about_landmark_text: The building at 435 Lawnmarket dates from the early 18th century, standing at the junction of the Lawnmarket and Bank Street, close to where William Brodie himself lived and kept his cabinet-making workshop. Its ground and first floors were converted into a public house by architect P. L. Henderson in 1894, with further alterations by Robert Hurd in 1950; it has been protected as a Category A listed building since 1970. Many tourist guides give 1806 as the tavern's founding date, though the listing record's account of a much later 1894 conversion suggests the pub in its current form may be somewhat younger than that popular figure.
about_subject_text: William Brodie (1741-1788) was a respected Edinburgh cabinet-maker, locksmith and city councillor who served as Deacon of the Incorporation of Wrights and Masons - a position of real civic standing. By night, he led a secret double life as a burglar, using his legitimate work fitting locks to take wax impressions of clients' keys. From 1786 he recruited accomplices for a string of break-ins, but a raid on the Excise Office at Chessels Court on 5 March 1788 went wrong, netting only around £16 before the gang was disturbed. Brodie fled first to London and then toward the Netherlands, where he was caught in Amsterdam and brought back to stand trial. He was hanged on 1 October 1788, reportedly before a huge crowd. Local legend holds that he had once helped design the very gallows used to hang him - a neat irony, even if it's hard to verify.
interesting_fact: The stark contrast between Brodie's respectable daytime reputation and his criminal double life is widely credited as an inspiration for Robert Louis Stevenson's Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886) - Stevenson grew up with a cabinet Brodie had built in his family home.

about_landmark_text: The Gatehouse forming Edinburgh Castle's main entrance looks centuries old but is a Victorian addition, built in 1886-88 in Scots Baronial style to give the fortress a grander, more romantic approach befitting its status as a national monument. Flanking the archway in twin canopied niches, added decades later in 1929 to mark the 600th anniversary of Robert the Bruce's death, stand bronze statues of Bruce and William Wallace; the drawbridge and portcullis groove above the arch are both still in working order.
about_subject_text: Funded by a bequest from Captain Hugh Reid and erected by the Corporation of Edinburgh, the statues were unveiled on 28 May 1929: Bruce, by sculptor Thomas J. Clapperton, wears his crown and carries an axe and shield; Wallace, by Alexander Carrick, grips a claymore. Both stand in niches designed by the architect Sir Robert Lorimer, who had designed the castle's own Scottish National War Memorial just a couple of years earlier, in 1927.
interesting_fact: Though it looks centuries old, the Gatehouse is actually a Victorian addition, built in 1886-88 - reportedly designed in some secrecy, since military authorities feared a cosmetic addition to a still-functioning garrison might draw public criticism.

about_landmark_text: Petit Paris opened in 1998 in a space that had previously housed one of the original branches of Pierre Victoire, the budget French bistro chain that collapsed the same year. It was founded by Philippe Bachelet, originally from Orleans, who had worked at Edinburgh's first Pierre Victoire since 1989 and later ran two Chez Jules franchises with his wife, Nathalie, before striking out on his own. Bachelet bought the building's freehold in 2004 and completed a self-funded refurbishment in 2011, fitting bespoke oak units while keeping the red-and-white gingham tablecloths and whitewashed walls that give the place its old-fashioned Parisian cafe feel. It remains an independent, family-run bistro serving classic French dishes such as coq au vin. Widely regarded as one of Edinburgh's best French restaurants, it holds a 4.5-star average across thousands of reviews and a place on Tripadvisor's list of the city's top French dining spots.
about_subject_text: The Grassmarket has been one of Edinburgh's principal marketplaces since it was formalised by royal charter under King James III in 1477, and a farmers' market still runs there today. For more than a century, from around 1660, it also served as the city's main site of public execution: over 100 Covenanters - Presbyterians who refused to accept the crown's authority over the Church of Scotland - were hanged here during the so-called Killing Times of the 1660s to 1680s. A cobblestone memorial pattern and a monument raised by public subscription in 1937 mark the site of the gallows today.
interesting_fact: Diners at Petit Paris's outdoor tables look straight up at Edinburgh Castle, perched on its rock directly above the square - one of the more dramatic backdrops for a plate of moules frites anywhere in the city.

about_landmark_text: Designed by George Washington Browne in an ornate French Renaissance style, Edinburgh Central Library opened on George IV Bridge in 1890 as the city's first public library. The building drops away below street level, with further storeys descending through the gorge towards the Cowgate. It stands on the site of a 1616 townhouse belonging to Sir Thomas Hope, whose carved stone lintel - inscribed 'TECUM HABITA 1616' - was preserved and set into the new building.
about_subject_text: The library was paid for by the Scottish-American steel magnate Andrew Carnegie, who doubled his original offer of £25,000 to £50,000 after being shown the site. Carnegie insisted the words 'Let there be Light' be carved above the entrance of every library he funded, and they appear above the door here too. He wasn't present when Lord Rosebery officially opened the building on 9 June 1890 - instead a telegram from Carnegie was read out, hoping 'that this Library is to grow in usefulness year after year.'
interesting_fact: Edinburgh is still the only local authority in the UK that classifies its adult library collection using the Library of Congress system rather than Dewey Decimal.

title: Greyfriars Bobby
clue_text: walk South East to find a statue of a loveable animal - but get the right one! -  dont forget to note what you see on the way, you will need it for the quiz
puzzle_question: How many years did the animal live for?
about_landmark_text: This life-size bronze statue and drinking fountain was sculpted by William Brodie and unveiled in 1873 at the junction of George IV Bridge and Candlemaker Row, opposite the entrance to Greyfriars Kirkyard. It was funded by the English philanthropist Baroness Angela Burdett-Coutts. Standing barely a foot tall, it's said to be the smallest listed structure in Edinburgh.
about_subject_text: Bobby was a small terrier - accounts differ on whether he was a Skye Terrier or a Dandie Dinmont - who belonged to John Gray, a nightwatchman with the Edinburgh City Police. When Gray died of tuberculosis in 1858 and was buried in Greyfriars Kirkyard, Bobby is said to have kept vigil at the grave for the next fourteen years, until his own death in 1872. The story is one of the most disputed in Edinburgh folklore: historian Jan Bondeson has pointed to more than sixty similar 'faithful graveyard dog' tales recorded across 19th-century Europe, and has suggested the original Bobby may have died around 1867, with a younger dog taking his place for the rest of the vigil.
interesting_fact: Edinburgh's Lord Provost, Sir William Chambers, was so taken with Bobby's story that in 1867 he personally paid for the dog's licence and had him fitted with a collar, now on display in the Museum of Edinburgh.

about_landmark_text: Designed by Sir Robert Rowand Anderson in an Italian Renaissance style, McEwan Hall is the University of Edinburgh's striking drum-shaped graduation hall, built through the late 1880s and 1890s and completed in 1897. Inside, a huge domed ceiling is covered in murals by William Mainwaring Palin depicting allegorical figures representing the Arts and Sciences, centred on a scene titled 'The Temple of Fame'. The hall's 1897 organ, built by Robert Hope-Jones, is one of only two of his instruments to survive in the UK.
about_subject_text: The hall was paid for almost entirely by William McEwan, a wealthy Edinburgh brewer and Liberal MP, who gave over £100,000 towards its construction - something in the region of £12-13 million today. McEwan had left school at 14 to work in his uncle's brewery and built it into one of Scotland's largest, later using his fortune to fund several university buildings. He appears among the allegorical figures painted into the hall's dome, alongside the arts and sciences he helped make room for.
interesting_fact: Rowand Anderson designed carved niches all around the building's exterior to hold statues - but the money ran out before any were ever installed, so they remain empty to this day.

title: Lt David Stuart McGregor VC
address: George Heriot's School boundary, Lauriston Place, Edinburgh EH3 9EZ
clue_text: head South-West for 500m - look for a memorial plaque - this one is VERY hard to find - about 12x12 inches - dont forget to note what you see on the way, you will need it for the quiz
puzzle_question: How many black posts are blocking the lane
about_landmark_text: This small commemorative plaque, produced jointly by the City of Edinburgh Council and the Scotland's War project, marks the life of Lieutenant David Stuart McGregor VC close to the two schools he attended. A separate stone memorial to McGregor was later unveiled at the boundary of George Heriot's School, on the corner of Lauriston Place and Heriot Place, on 22 October 2018 - the centenary of his death.
about_subject_text: Born in Corstorphine on 16 October 1895, McGregor was educated at George Watson's College and George Heriot's School before joining the Commercial Bank of Scotland as an apprentice. He joined the 6th Royal Scots in 1915, serving in Egypt before being attached to the 29th Battalion, Machine Gun Corps in France. On 22 October 1918, near Hoogemolen, Belgium, his unit came under intense machine-gun fire while advancing. McGregor located the enemy guns, then rode a limber forward under fire for around 600 yards to get his own guns into action and cover the advance - he was killed shortly afterwards, on his 23rd birthday. He is buried at Stasegem Communal Cemetery in Belgium; his parents received his Victoria Cross from King George V at Buckingham Palace on 15 February 1919.
interesting_fact: McGregor's Victoria Cross was eventually donated to the Royal Scots Museum at Edinburgh Castle in 1976, where it remains on display today.

title: The Wee Pub - Smallest Pub in Scotland
clue_text: head along Heriot Place until you come to familiar ground - then look for a pub, but not a big one - dont forget to note what you see on the way, you will need it for the quiz

about_landmark_text: Opened in 2013 as a snug extension of Biddy Mulligans next door, the Wee Pub has its own entrance onto the Grassmarket but shares its staff and stock with the bar beside it. It fits around twenty people 'at a push', with just enough room inside for a small fireplace and a dresser-style bar, making it one of the tiniest working pubs anywhere in Scotland.
about_subject_text: The square outside has been a marketplace since at least 1477, trading livestock and goods in the shadow of the Castle rock. It has a much darker history too: over 100 people were hanged here between 1661 and 1688, many of them Covenanters executed during 'the Killing Time', and a memorial to their deaths still stands nearby. In 1724, Margaret 'Maggie' Dickson was hanged in the Grassmarket for concealing a pregnancy, survived the ordeal after being cut down, and lived on as 'Half-Hangit Maggie' - one of Edinburgh's most retold legends.
interesting_fact: The drinks menu here is printed on a single postcard - small enough that a magnifying glass is kept behind the bar so customers can actually read it.
